chapterTitle: What ByteBook is, and what this handbook is for
title: What ByteBook is, and what this handbook is for
text: ByteBook is a bookkeeping program for New Zealand businesses. It keeps the whole set of books in one file on the computer it runs on. It records invoices and bills, imports a bank statement and codes every line, works out the GST return, and produces the reports an accountant or an auditor asks for. It also does something most bookkeeping programs do not. Every entry is sealed with a fingerprint when it is written, and the record can never be quietly changed: a mistake is voided , which posts the mirror image of the entry and leaves both in the books. Anyone can then re-run the checks and see for themselves that the books still add up. That is what makes ByteBook useful for training auditors as well as bookkeepers.

chapterTitle: What ByteBook is, and what this handbook is for
title: Why there is a handbook
text: Most bookkeeping training happens on a live client's file, or on a spreadsheet invented for the lesson. Neither is ideal. A live file punishes a wrong click with a real consequence; a spreadsheet does not behave like a set of books. It has no GST return, no bank reconciliation and no audit trail, so the parts that are actually hard to learn are missing. ByteBook ships with twelve practice businesses. Each one is a New Zealand business with months of trading already in the books: a hairdresser who is not registered for GST, a builder taking stage payments, a café banking its takings, an online store handling credits and reversals, a landlord with exempt rent, a horticulture contractor on a six-monthly GST cycle, a software company with costs and no income, a dental practice where roles matter. Open any of them from Practice businesses in the app. They are copies kept beside your own books, so nothing you do in one can touch your records, and Start over puts a business back the way it was. Nothing you do in training can damage a client's records, because there is no client. This handbook is the course that goes with it. It covers the daily work — sending an invoice, coding a bank lin

chapterTitle: What ByteBook is, and what this handbook is for
title: Who it is for
text: New accounting staff. You will do the work in a business that behaves like a real one, where a payment arrives late, a bill is paid twice, and the bank statement does not agree at the first try. Audit staff in training. You will meet the sixteen procedures an auditor runs, learn what each one is for, and see what the exception looks like when the books are wrong. Students. Every topic here is a topic in a New Zealand accounting or taxation paper, seen from the inside rather than from a textbook. The person running the training. Every exercise has a marking note, and the twelve sessions in Part 5 can be handed out as they are.

chapterTitle: What ByteBook is, and what this handbook is for
title: Three ways to use it
text: 1. Read it straight through. The chapters follow the order a month actually happens in: set up, trade, bank, file, report, then check. 2. Work through it with the program open. Each chapter has steps to carry out in ByteBook. The work is where the learning is; the reading only gets you to the right screen. 3. Use it as a reference. The glossary explains the terms in plain words, and every standard is listed in the reference index with the screen it belongs to.

chapterTitle: What ByteBook is, and what this handbook is for
title: What this handbook is not
text: Being clear about this saves trouble later. It is not tax advice. ByteBook works out GST figures from your own transactions and lays them out in the boxes Inland Revenue asks for. Whether a particular sale is taxable is a question about a particular business. It does not replace the standards. It points at them, quotes a few words where the words matter, and names the paragraph. Read the standard itself before you rely on it. Every reference in this handbook carries the address of the publisher's document and the fingerprint of the copy we read. It does not replace professional judgement. An auditor does not conclude from a tick list. ByteBook reports what it found and leaves the conclusion to the person; this handbook does the same. It is written for New Zealand. The standards referenced are New Zealand's: NZ IFRS, which carry international accounting standards with New Zealand additions, and the ISAs (NZ), which carry the international auditing standards with New Zealand additions. chapterTitle: Set up a training business
title: Install it
text: On a Mac , open the ByteBook disk image and drag ByteBook into Applications. That is the whole install. The program carries everything it needs, so it works on a computer with nothing else on it and with the internet switched off. On Windows , run the installer and follow it. It installs for your own user account, so it does not need an administrator password, and it leaves a ByteBook shortcut in the Start menu. The Windows build is an unsigned beta, so Windows may warn you the first time; the download page publishes a SHA-256 checksum you can check the file against. On a Mac the application is signed with ByteMind's Apple Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so there is nothing to click through: it opens on a Mac that has never seen it, with the internet switched off.

chapterTitle: Set up a training business
title: Answer four short questions
text: The first time ByteBook opens, it runs four short steps and then leaves you alone. You can change any answer later in Settings . 1. Your business. Its name and contact details, which print on every document. Use a pretend name for training — keeping the practice business separate from a real one matters more than it sounds. 2. GST and your balance date. Whether you are registered for GST, how often you file, whether you are on the invoice basis or the payments basis, and the date your financial year ends. These decide whether GST appears on a document and which return period a transaction falls in. 3. How you invoice. The prefix for invoice numbers and how many days a customer has to pay. (The note at the foot of an invoice is set later under Settings → Invoices .) 4. You are ready. A short checklist, and the button that opens the books. Learning to find and correct one of these settings is part of the exercise: they all live under Settings afterwards.

chapterTitle: Set up a training business
title: Practice on a business that already exists
text: Setting up a business from nothing teaches you the setting up. It does not teach you what it is like to open somebody's books in the middle of a year, which is the situation most of this handbook is really about. Practice businesses — in the sidebar under Set up — are twelve New Zealand businesses with months of trading already in their books. Each one is a different trade, and each trade brings its own kind of question: Business Trade What it is there to teach --- --- --- Bright Cuts Hairdressing A business below the GST threshold, with no tax on anything Kōwhai Advisory Consulting GST on the payments basis, where the tax follows the money Tasman Builders Ltd Construction Stage payments over months, where ageing matters more than the total Harbour Cafe & Co Hospitality Daily takings banked in a lump, and the difference somebody has to explain Loom & Light Online retail Refunds and reversals, which are not negative sales Marine Parade Rentals Residential property Exempt rent, and repairs you cannot claim GST on Whirinaki Contracting Horticulture Seasonal work on a six-monthly GST period Foundry Labs Software A year of costs and no income, funded by somebody else Marine Parade Denta

chapterTitle: Set up a training business
title: Give yourself a role
text: By default ByteBook opens without a password, which is right for a computer only one person uses. For training it is better to switch security on, because the roles are part of what you are here to learn: Role May do --- --- Owner Everything, including settings, backups and who can sign in General manager Run the books: invoices, bills, bank, GST, reports Accountant Read everything, including the tax working papers; change nothing Auditor Read the books and the assurance work, change nothing Turn on Settings → Security , set your own password first, then add the other roles. ByteBook will not switch anyone else's access on until the owner has a password, so a login cannot be handed out that locks the owner out. The distinction between reading and changing is the point. An auditor who cannot change the books is not a technical detail; it is the arrangement that makes the audit worth anything. :::aside Why the roles are built this way An assurance practitioner is required to comply with the principle of objectivity, which means exercising judgement without being compromised by bias, a conflict of interest or undue influence PES 1 R112.1. chapterTitle: Set up a training business
title: The assistant, if you switch it on
text: The assistant is off by default, and while it is off ByteBook never contacts anyone. Settings → Assistant switches it on: choose a provider, add an API key, and press Test connection , which sends one tiny request and nothing from your books. The key is kept outside your books, in the operating system's secure store where there is one, so a backup of the books does not carry the key with it. If a key looks incomplete after you paste it, ByteBook tells you on the same page instead of failing quietly later — paste the whole key and save again. What a request sends is limited to what the question needs: account names and balances, plus customer names only when you ask it to draft an invoice. Bank account numbers and contact details are not sent. With a local model (Ollama), nothing leaves the computer at all. The assistant explains and drafts; it does not post entries. Every figure it quotes comes from the page you were looking at, so it can be checked there.

chapterTitle: Set up a training business
title: Know where the books are
text: The whole bookkeeping record is one file. On a Mac it lives in ~/Library/Application Support/ByteBook/ ; on Windows it lives in %APPDATA%\ByteBook\ . Beside it is a backups folder that keeps the last thirty copies. That single file is worth understanding before you start. Backing up a set of books is copying one file. Moving them to another computer is copying one file. Nothing in it is locked to ByteBook, although reading it without the program needs a database viewer. It also means the fingerprint chain described in chapter 12 has something to protect: the record is a file on a disk, and the chain is what tells you whether anyone has edited it.

chapterTitle: The twelve businesses you can practise on
title: Open one
text: 1. In the sidebar, under Set up , choose Practice businesses . 2. Read what each business is there to teach. Under What to try there are four things worth doing in that business. 3. Press Start this business . ByteBook closes and opens again on that business's books, and a line at the top of every page says which business you are in. Your own books are never touched. A practice business is a copy kept beside them, and the line at the top of the page is how you always know which set you are looking at.

chapterTitle: The twelve businesses you can practise on
title: Come back, or start again
text: Back to my books. The line at the top of every page has this button. It closes the practice business and opens your own books again. Continue. If you have already worked in a business, the button says Continue and it picks up where you left off. Work you do in a practice business is kept. Start over. This puts the business back exactly as it was, ready for the next person. You cannot start over the business you are currently in — open another one, or your own books, first. Save a copy of these books. Downloads the practice business as an ordinary ByteBook file, which you can open from Practice businesses → Open your own books from a file .

chapterTitle: The twelve businesses you can practise on
title: What is already true of all twelve
text: Every one of these businesses is complete and internally consistent. Before they shipped, each was traded through the real application and then checked from the raw rows: every entry balances, so money in equals money out; every invoice's lines add up to its total; the GST in the return equals the GST in the ledger; the balance sheet balances; nothing is stored off the cent; a voided entry cancels itself out; the fingerprint chain has no breaks; the assurance programme reports no exceptions (it may still carry notes for information). That last point can sound odd in a training business. It is deliberate. What is waiting in these books is the ordinary work of a business — invoices past their due date, a bill still to pay, a draft invoice to finish, a bank reconciliation to check — not a planted mistake. Your job is to do the work and read the evidence, not to hunt for something the program has hidden.

chapterTitle: The twelve businesses you can practise on
title: Why this matters more than it sounds
text: A rule that is easy to state is often hard to apply. Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value NZ IAS 2.9 is one sentence. Knowing when a selling price has fallen far enough that the book value has to come down is a judgement, and judgement needs practice on something that behaves like a real business. The awkward cases are in these books on purpose: a customer who pays late, so the aged debtors report has something in it; two identical-looking payments to the same supplier, which you have to check are genuinely two payments (A03 lists identical lines for you to check, and A08 looks for the same amount described the same way twice in a week); a manual journal, which an auditor will ask about; a bank statement that has to be reconciled, with a closing balance that has to come from the statement rather than from the ledger; a period that can be sealed, and then checked again later.

chapterTitle: The twelve businesses you can practise on
title: Choosing where to start
text: If you are new to bookkeeping, start with Kōwhai Advisory (consulting). It is a small business with ordinary transactions and one late payment. If you are here for the audit side, start with Ngata Plumbing Ltd (trades). A busy bank statement produces more coding decisions, more places to make a mistake, and a more interesting reconciliation. If you are teaching, use Precision Engineering Ltd last. It is built from the amounts that break careless rounding, and it shows why money has to be kept in whole cents: a cent cannot go missing when amounts are added. :::check 1. Which business has no GST at all, and which one has exempt rent beside its other income? 2. Name three things that are already consistent in every practice business. 3. Why does a six-monthly GST cycle make for a harder exercise than a monthly one? :::

chapterTitle: Invoices: selling on paper and in the books
title: What an invoice does
text: An invoice does two separate things, and keeping them separate prevents most of the confusion in this chapter. 1. It is a document. It goes to a customer, it shows what was supplied, what it cost, how much GST is included, and when payment is due. ByteBook prints it with your letterhead, and the same page can be saved as a PDF or posted. 2. It is an accounting entry. When the invoice is posted, the books record money owed to you, the revenue you have earned, and the GST you have collected. You can create an invoice as a draft , which does the first job and not the second. A draft is a document you can still change. Nothing in your reports moves until you post it. That distinction is the single most useful thing to understand about the Invoices screen.

chapterTitle: Invoices: selling on paper and in the books
title: Raise one
text: 1. Go to Invoices → New invoice . 2. Choose the customer. If they are not there, add them first under Customers & suppliers . Their GST number, if you record it, prints on the invoice, but it is not what makes the invoice valid: a tax invoice has to show your own GST number. 3. Add the lines: what you supplied, the quantity, and the price. 4. Decide how the price is expressed. ByteBook stores every amount excluding GST and holds the GST separately, so no report ever has to guess which way a number was meant. Choose Yes — the price already includes GST if the price you were given already includes it, and ByteBook will take the GST out. 5. Put it in my books now is already ticked. Leave it ticked to post the invoice immediately, or untick it to keep the invoice as a draft.

chapterTitle: Invoices: selling on paper and in the books
title: When revenue is recognised
text: This is where the accounting standard earns its place, and it is worth reading slowly. Revenue is recognised when the business satisfies a performance obligation by transferring a promised good or service to the customer NZ IFRS 15.31. Not when the invoice is raised, not when the money arrives: when the promise is kept. For most small businesses, those three dates are close enough together that the distinction does not bite. It bites in these cases: Stage payments on a contract. The Tasman Builders practice business raises several invoices for one job. Each invoice recognises revenue for the work it covers, because that is the work that has been transferred. A deposit taken before any work is done. Money received is not revenue yet. It is money you owe back in services. A service delivered in March and invoiced in April. The revenue belongs in March. ByteBook will not stop you from posting an invoice on the wrong date. It records the date you enter, and the reports follow it. Choosing the right date is the job.

chapterTitle: Invoices: selling on paper and in the books
title: What posting does to the books
text: Posting an invoice creates one balanced entry. Three things happen at once: Side What it means --- --- Money owed to you goes up An asset. The customer owes the business Revenue goes up Income, recorded excluding GST GST collected goes up A liability you owe Inland Revenue, not income The last line is the one people get wrong by hand. GST collected on a sale is never income. It is money held on behalf of Inland Revenue until the return is filed, which is why ByteBook keeps it in its own account and reports it in box 8 of the return. :::aside What the standards say A complete set of financial statements includes a statement of financial position, a statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, a statement of changes in equity, a statement of cash flows and notes NZ IAS 1.10. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions NZ IAS 1.15. An invoice that puts revenue in the wrong period is not a rounding difference — it is a failure of faithful representation, and it is exactly what a cut-off procedure is designed to find (see chapter 13). :::

chapterTitle: Invoices: selling on paper and in the books
title: Common mistakes
text: Treating GST collected as income. Check that revenue in the profit and loss report is the figure excluding GST. Raising an invoice and assuming it is in the books. Look for the word draft . A draft is a document, not an entry. Entering a GST-inclusive price as if it excluded GST. The invoice then overstates revenue by the GST. ByteBook's totals make the error visible: the invoice total will not match the amount you agreed with the customer.

chapterTitle: Invoices: selling on paper and in the books
title: In the transaction list
text: Every posted invoice appears under Transactions with its own entry, and the entry shows both sides. Open one and read it. Learning to read the entry behind the document is the skill this screen exists to teach, and an auditor who cannot read the entry behind a document is stuck at the first question. :::check 1. A customer pays a deposit in June for work done in August. When is the revenue recognised, and why? 2. What does posting an invoice change, and what does leaving it as a draft change? 3. ByteBook stores prices excluding GST. What problem does that solve? :::

chapterTitle: Payments, and the money you are owed
title: Recording a payment
text: When money arrives, open the invoice and use the payment box. ByteBook applies the amount against the invoice, marks it paid or part-paid, and posts an entry that moves money from owed to you into the bank. Part payments work the same way. Record what actually arrived. If a customer short-pays because of a dispute, the balance stays on the invoice, and the debtors report keeps showing it, which is how the question gets asked.

chapterTitle: Payments, and the money you are owed
title: What the aged debtors list is for
text: Reports → Who owes what lists what customers owe, grouped by how long it has been owed. It is not a statement about whether the money will arrive. It is a statement about what has been invoiced and not yet paid, and it is the starting point for two different jobs: Chasing the money. ByteBook can draft a reminder letter for any unpaid invoice. The text is a starting point; the relationship is yours. Judging whether the money is real. A debt that is not going to be paid is not an asset worth its face value.

chapterTitle: Payments, and the money you are owed
title: The second question: will it be paid?
text: This is where a bookkeeping exercise turns into an accounting judgement. Trade receivables are measured at an amount that reflects the cash the business expects to collect, and for trade receivables the loss allowance is measured at lifetime expected credit losses NZ IFRS 9 5.5.15. In plain words: for money owed by customers, you start from the assumption that some of it will not be paid, and you estimate how much. The usual approach in a small business is a provision matrix . Group the debtors by age, apply a percentage to each group based on experience, and add the results: Age Typical treatment --- --- Current No allowance, or a very small one 1–30 days past due A small percentage 31–90 days past due A larger percentage Over 90 days A large percentage, or the whole amount Identified as bad The whole amount Two things make this a professional judgement rather than arithmetic. The percentages have to come from somewhere — the business's own history, or industry experience — and a specific debt known to be bad is written off in full whatever the age table says.

chapterTitle: Payments, and the money you are owed
title: What the auditor asks next
text: An auditor does not take the debtors list at face value. The main procedure is external confirmation : asking the customer, directly, whether they agree that they owe the amount. Where the answer raises doubt about its reliability, the auditor has to obtain further evidence to resolve it ISA 505.10. In the practice businesses, the debtors procedure reports: how much is owed and how much of it is late; any document that looks overpaid, which usually means a payment went to the wrong invoice or was recorded twice; the invoices that have been owed for more than 90 days. The procedure reports what it found. Whether a 90-day debt will be paid is a question for a person, and ByteBook does not pretend otherwise. :::aside What the standard says For trade receivables, the loss allowance is always measured at an amount equal to lifetime expected credit losses NZ IFRS 9 5.5.15. The judgement is in the estimate, not in whether to make one. :::

chapterTitle: Payments, and the money you are owed
title: Common mistakes
text: Recording a payment against the wrong invoice. The total owed is right and the ageing is wrong, which hides a real problem. Check the invoice number on the remittance. Treating a part payment as full settlement. ByteBook keeps the balance open, and that is correct. Writing off a debt by deleting the invoice. ByteBook will not let you delete it, and that is also correct: the record of the sale and the record of the loss are both part of the history. Void the invoice, or post the write-off as an expense, and the trail stays readable. Leaving the allowance at last year's percentage without looking. The estimate is meant to describe this year's debts. Leaving a payment against the wrong invoice. Open the invoice, choose Reverse the payment , and record it against the right one. The correction stays in the record beside the mistake, and the invoice can then be voided if it should never have been raised. :::check 1. A customer pays $500 against a $1,200 invoice. What does the aged debtors list show, and why is that right? 2. Why is a credit balance in the debtors list worth investigating? 3. What does the standard require for trade receivables, and what is left to judgement? :::

chapterTitle: Bills, expenses and the documents behind them
title: Two kinds of outgoing
text: Money leaving a business arrives in two shapes, and ByteBook keeps them apart: A bill. An invoice from a supplier, with a due date, that you will pay later. Record it under Bills to pay . Until it is paid it sits in creditors. An expense paid now. Money that has already left the bank. Usually you meet these while coding the bank statement, in chapter 7. Both end up in the same place: an expense in the profit and loss report, and a GST credit if the purchase carried GST.

chapterTitle: Bills, expenses and the documents behind them
title: Record a bill
text: 1. Go to Bills to pay → Record a bill . 2. Choose the supplier. Add the supplier's GST number to the contact if it is missing. It is needed on their tax invoice, and ByteBook's documents procedure reports the ones that do not have it. 3. Enter the lines, and mark whether the amounts include GST. 4. Save. The bill is now in creditors, and the expense is in the books. 5. Pay it when the money leaves, from the bill itself, so the payment and the bill stay linked.

chapterTitle: Bills, expenses and the documents behind them
title: The document, not just the number
text: For a bookkeeping record to be worth anything, each figure has to be traceable to the document behind it. Inland Revenue's rule is practical: a tax invoice for more than $50 has to show the supplier's GST number, among other things. ByteBook's documents procedure checks for that and reports the documents that have something missing. An auditor's version of the same question is in the auditing standard on audit evidence: the auditor designs and performs procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances for obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence ISA 500.6, and considers the relevance and reliability of the information used as evidence ISA 500.7. A supplier's own tax invoice is stronger evidence than a note in a diary.

chapterTitle: Bills, expenses and the documents behind them
title: Getting the expense in the right period
text: An expense belongs in the period the business consumed whatever it paid for, not the period the money left the bank. Two common cases: A bill received in March for February's electricity. The expense belongs in February, when the power was used, even though the bill arrived in March. Post it with February's date. A payment in April for a service covering April to June. Part of it belongs in a later period. That part is a prepayment. Procedure A11 lists the large one-off costs where these questions have to be asked; deciding whether a cost is personal or an asset is yours, not the program's. If a figure is found to be wrong after the financial statements were issued, material prior period errors are corrected retrospectively NZ IAS 8.42. If the business changed an estimate — how long a machine will last, for instance — the effect is recognised prospectively, in this period and later ones NZ IAS 8.36. An error and a change in estimate are different things, and they are accounted for differently, which is why the distinction is worth learning early.

chapterTitle: Bills, expenses and the documents behind them
title: Expenses an auditor looks at twice
text: The expenses procedure in ByteBook is deliberately blunt. It reports the three patterns where an expense account is most often wrong: Round numbers. A $1,000 payment described as "sundry" is a question, not an answer. Large one-off costs. Above about $1,000, the question is whether it was an expense at all, or something the business now owns. An item of property, plant and equipment that qualifies for recognition is measured at its cost NZ IAS 16.15, and depreciation begins when it is available for use NZ IAS 16.55, not when it was paid for. Costs that look personal. These matter for two reasons: they may not be deductible, and if the owner took value out of the company this way, the transaction may be with a related party.

chapterTitle: Bills, expenses and the documents behind them
title: Related parties
text: A small company's transactions with its owners and their other businesses are related party transactions, and they get special attention because they are where the interests of the business and the interests of an individual can diverge. An auditor is required to inquire of management about the identity of the entity's related parties, including changes from the prior period, and about the nature of the relationships and transactions ISA 550.13. In practice: if the business paid money to a person or a company connected with the owner, say so, and keep the paperwork. :::check 1. A bill arrives in March for February's power. The payment leaves in April. When is the expense recorded, and why? 2. What is the difference in treatment between a change in estimate and a prior period error? 3. A $2,400 payment to a supplier is described as "sundry expenses". What should you check first? :::

chapterTitle: The bank statement, line by line
title: Why this chapter matters most
text: The bank statement is where the books meet the outside world. It is also where most small-business bookkeeping errors live, because coding a bank line is a judgement made quickly, hundreds of times. Get this screen right and the rest follows: the GST return falls out of the coded transactions, the reports are sums of real rows, and the reconciliation tells you whether you are finished. Get it wrong and every later figure is wrong in a way that is hard to see.

chapterTitle: The bank statement, line by line
title: Import
text: Download a CSV from your internet banking, then open Bank & coding , choose Import a bank statement , pick the file and say which account it came from. ByteBook reads the columns, works out which is the date, the description and the amount, and skips anything that has already been imported, so importing the same file twice does not double the books. Two identical lines in one statement are kept as two lines: two coffees on the same day are two coffees. Only a re-import is skipped. If your bank's export looks unusual, the page offers a CSV template showing the shape ByteBook expects.

chapterTitle: The bank statement, line by line
title: Code each line
text: Every imported line is a question: what was this for? You answer by choosing an account. ByteBook guesses from the description, and you confirm or correct it. Three answers are possible: Code it to an account. The line becomes a real transaction in the books. Mark it as not business. The line stays on the statement and out of the reports. A personal coffee on the business account belongs here, or better, it belongs in drawings. Leave it waiting. Nothing in the reports moves until you decide. The screen tells you how many lines are waiting. Until that number is zero, the books are incomplete, and a report run now is a report on part of the period.

chapterTitle: The bank statement, line by line
title: Does it agree with your bank?
text: There is a second half to the screen, and it is the one that turns coding into assurance. Enter the closing balance and the date from your bank statement, and ByteBook compares its own bank balance with the bank's figure. Two agreements matter. The bank agrees. The balance ByteBook holds for the bank account equals the balance on the statement at the statement's date. ByteBook remembers the last balance and date you entered, so check they are current: an old closing balance produces a difference that is a stale note, not a bookkeeping error. If it does not, either something has not been recorded, or something has been recorded twice, or the date is wrong. This is bank reconciliation, and it is procedure A03 in chapter 13. Every line has been dealt with. The number waiting to be coded is zero, and nothing has been left in a half-finished state. A reconciliation that matches on the balance but has twenty uncoded lines is not a reconciliation.

chapterTitle: The bank statement, line by line
title: Why the reconciliation is evidence
text: An auditor treats a bank confirmation as strong evidence, because the answer comes from outside the business. The auditing standard on external confirmations deals with the auditor's use of a confirmation request, and requires further evidence where the reliability of a response is in doubt ISA 505.10. The statement you import is the same kind of evidence: it was produced by the bank, not by the business. That is why the reconciliation is worth doing even when the balance already looks right. It is not arithmetic housekeeping. It is the test that ties the books to something outside them. :::aside A reconciliation is not a report Reports describe. A reconciliation tests . The difference is that a test can fail, and when it fails it tells you something specific: the books and the bank disagree, by this amount, at this date. Learning to read the size and direction of a difference is most of the skill. :::

chapterTitle: The bank statement, line by line
title: Common mistakes
text: Coding a line to the wrong side. A payment received coded as an expense cancels the error in the total while leaving the GST and the customer balance wrong. Choosing the wrong GST treatment for the account. The bank line is what left the account, GST included, and ByteBook always takes the GST out of that amount. What it needs from you is the account the money was really for, because that decides whether the payment carries GST at all. Reconciling to the wrong date. Agree the balance at the statement's date, not at today's date. Marking a business line as not business to clear the list. The waiting count goes down and the books get worse. If you are unsure, leave it waiting and find out. :::check 1. The reconciliation balances but eleven lines are still waiting to be coded. Is the reconciliation finished? Explain. 2. Why is the bank statement stronger evidence than a note in the business's own diary? 3. A bank line of $1,150 is a payment to a supplier. What does ByteBook need to know before it can decide whether the payment carries GST? :::

chapterTitle: GST: the return built from your own transactions
title: What the GST screen does
text: Open GST and ByteBook shows the return for the period you choose, built from the transactions in your books. Nothing is typed in twice and nothing is estimated: every box is a sum of coded entries, and every figure can be traced back to the transactions that produced it. The boxes you will meet: Box What it is --- --- 5 Total sales and income, including GST 6 Zero-rated supplies included in box 5 8 GST on sales 11 Total purchases and expenses, including GST 12 GST on purchases 15 GST to pay, or refund due The numbers are those on the GST101A return you file in myIR, and ByteBook labels its figures with the same numbers. Box 5 includes income that carries no GST, such as interest, because the return asks for total sales and income. Box 8 is the GST itself. Keeping those two apart is the point of the box structure, and mixing them up is the most common GST error in small-business records.

chapterTitle: GST: the return built from your own transactions
title: Work out a period
text: 1. Choose the period. ByteBook offers the cycles that match your filing frequency, and you can set any start and end date. 2. Press Recalculate . The boxes fill in from the ledger. 3. Read the Result : GST on sales less GST on purchases, which is box 15, the amount to pay or the refund due. 4. Check the period against the ledger before you go further. The GST reconciliation procedure (A06) checks that the GST in the return is the GST in the ledger, transaction by transaction. 5. Save this as a snapshot. The snapshot is a record of what you filed, at the date you worked it out, and it stays after the transactions move on. 6. Mark as filed once you have entered the figures in myIR. If the ledger is changed later, ByteBook warns that the filed period no longer matches what was filed.

chapterTitle: GST: the return built from your own transactions
title: Invoice basis and payments basis
text: The basis you chose when you set the business up decides which transactions fall inside a period: Invoice basis. GST is accounted for when the invoice is issued or received, whether or not the money has moved. A sale invoiced in March is in the March period even if the customer pays in May. Payments basis. GST is accounted for when money actually moves. The same March invoice belongs in the period the payment arrived. Most small businesses can use the payments basis; larger ones cannot. The choice changes the figures in every period, and it is the reason two businesses with identical invoices can have different returns. ByteBook works the return out on the basis in your settings, and the basis is shown beside the figures. Read it before you read the numbers: a figure without its basis is a figure you cannot check, and changing the basis can move the same transactions to a different period.

chapterTitle: GST: the return built from your own transactions
title: When a sale carries no GST
text: Not every sale is taxable. The Marine Parade Rentals practice business earns exempt rent beside taxable supplies. Exempt income appears in box 5 as income, contributes nothing to box 8, and does not entitle the business to claim GST on costs that relate to it. This is where a bookkeeping exercise becomes a tax question, and it is worth being plain about the limit: ByteBook adds up what you coded. Whether rent, a particular financial service or a going concern is taxable, zero-rated or exempt is a question about the specific supply, and Inland Revenue's own guidance is the authority for it. Getting the treatment wrong is easy to do and expensive to fix.

chapterTitle: GST: the return built from your own transactions
title: A note on income tax
text: GST is not income tax, and the two should never be mixed in your thinking. GST is a tax on the supply of goods and services, collected by the business on Inland Revenue's behalf. Income tax is a tax on profit. A GST return says nothing about whether the business made money. For income tax, ByteBook prepares the working papers: Reports → IRD working papers builds the IR3, IR10 and IR4 figures from the same ledger. Current tax is measured at the amount expected to be paid to the taxation authorities, using the tax rates and laws that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the reporting date NZ IAS 12.46.

chapterTitle: GST: the return built from your own transactions
title: Common mistakes
text: Filing before every bank line is coded. The return is built from transactions. A line still waiting is a transaction the return has not seen. Recording a GST-inclusive figure as the GST amount. At 15%, the GST inside a GST-inclusive amount is three twenty-thirds of it: $15 in $115. ByteBook works that split for you. Reading box 5 as though it were box 8 is the mistake to avoid. Filing without saving a snapshot. Then there is no record of what was filed, and the reconciliation has nothing to compare against. If the ledger is changed later, ByteBook warns that a filed period no longer matches its snapshot — read that warning, because the return you filed and the books you now hold disagree. Filing on the wrong basis. The basis is a setting, not a rule of bookkeeping. Check the word beside the figures before signing the return. Treating a refund as negative sales in the wrong period. A credit note or a refund reverses the sale it corrects, and the period it lands in matters. :::check 1. A sale is invoiced in March and paid in May. On the invoice basis, which return does it appear in? On the payments basis? 2. What is the difference between box 5 and box 8, and why does the distinction

chapterTitle: Reports: what each one answers
title: One report, one question
text: ByteBook's main reports are deliberately narrow. Each one answers a single question, and knowing which question saves a lot of time. Report The question it answers --- --- Profit and loss Did the business make money in this period? Balance sheet What does it own and owe, as at this date? Trial balance Do the accounts add up, and does the ledger balance? General ledger What happened in this account, entry by entry? Money in and out Where did the money come from and go? Who owes what Who owes us, and who do we owe?

chapterTitle: Reports: what each one answers
title: Profit and loss
text: Income less expenses for a period. Income is recorded excluding GST, because GST collected was never the business's money. One choice matters more than it looks. Expenses can be analysed by nature — what was bought, such as wages, rent, power — or by function — what the cost was for, such as cost of sales and administration. The standard requires one or the other, whichever provides information that is reliable and more relevant NZ IAS 1.99. ByteBook's chart of accounts is arranged by nature, which suits a small business and is easy to check.

chapterTitle: Reports: what each one answers
title: Balance sheet
text: Assets, liabilities and equity at a date, and the arithmetic that has to hold: assets − liabilities = equity ByteBook computes that difference and states it on the page. If it is not zero, the page says so rather than hiding it. A balance sheet that does not balance is not a presentation problem; something is wrong in the ledger, and the figures are not usable until it is found. The statement of financial position has to include certain line items where they are relevant, such as property, plant and equipment, inventories, trade and other receivables, cash, and trade and other payables NZ IAS 1.54. ByteBook groups its accounts to present them, and the general ledger is where you go when you want to see what is inside a line.

chapterTitle: Reports: what each one answers
title: Trial balance and general ledger
text: The trial balance is every account with its balance, and the check that total debits equal total credits. It is the fastest way to find that something is wrong. The general ledger is the detail. Pick an account and see every entry that touched it, in order. When a report figure looks wrong, this is where the answer is: not in the report, which is a sum, but in the rows that were summed.

chapterTitle: Reports: what each one answers
title: Money in and out
text: Profit and cash are different things, and Money in and out is where the difference starts to show. ByteBook's report lists the money that actually arrived and left each month, and the balance it leaves in the bank. That is the raw material of a cash flow statement, not the finished statement. A full statement of cash flows classifies every movement as operating, investing or financing NZ IAS 7.10, and is prepared using either the direct method or the indirect method NZ IAS 7.18. Transactions that involve no cash are left out of it and disclosed separately NZ IAS 7.43. A vehicle bought with a loan is the classic example: a real transaction, no cash, so it has to be disclosed rather than shown as a payment. ByteBook does not build that classified statement. For a small business, the "money in and out" list plus the profit and loss and balance sheet is usually enough to answer the question. Where a full statement is needed — a lender, a sale, a formal set of financial statements — the classification is done from these reports.

chapterTitle: Reports: what each one answers
title: Checking a report rather than trusting it
text: Every report in ByteBook is a sum of the entries in the ledger. The final assurance procedure, A14, goes further: it rebuilds the trial balance from the raw rows, checks debits equal credits, and recomputes the balance-sheet difference that the page reports. This check exists because there are two different ways for a number to be wrong. The books can be wrong — a transaction coded to the wrong account — and the report can be wrong, through a defect in the program that builds it. The first is a bookkeeping problem; the second is a reporting problem, and no amount of careful coding will fix it. A figure you cannot reproduce from the rows underneath it is not yet evidence. :::check 1. Why is income in the profit and loss report shown excluding GST? 2. ByteBook's balance sheet states the difference between assets and liabilities plus equity. Why show a figure that should always be zero? 3. A vehicle is bought with a bank loan. What appears in Money in and out , and why? :::

chapterTitle: Closing a month and a year
title: A closing routine
text: Closing a period is not an accounting event managers attend to. It is a short list of checks, done in order, that ends with a set of books you would be willing to hand to someone else. 1. Every bank line is coded. The waiting count on Bank & coding is zero. 2. The bank agrees. Reconcile to the statement's closing balance and date. 3. Outstanding items are current. Look at who owes you and who you owe. Anything long overdue is either a collection problem or a recording problem. 4. Prepayments and accruals are posted. Money paid in advance for a later period, and costs incurred but not yet invoiced. 5. Depreciation is posted. For each class of asset, the depreciable amount is allocated on a systematic basis over its useful life NZ IAS 16.50. 6. Provisions are reviewed. A provision is recognised where there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable, and the amount can be estimated reliably NZ IAS 37.14. 7. The GST period is saved as a snapshot and marked as filed. 8. The reports are reproduced. Run the assurance procedures and confirm that the figures on the reports can be recalculated from the rows. 9. The period is sealed. See chapter 14. 10. A backup is take

chapterTitle: Closing a month and a year
title: Inventories, if the business holds any
text: Inventories are measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value NZ IAS 2.9. Cost includes the costs of purchase, the costs of conversion and the other costs incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition NZ IAS 2.10, and it is assigned using first-in, first-out or a weighted average NZ IAS 2.25. Net realisable value is the estimated selling price less the estimated costs of completion and sale. Where cost is not recoverable — damaged stock, or stock whose selling price has fallen — the write-down is recognised as an expense in the period it happens NZ IAS 2.28. The Pacific Trading practice business trades inventory, so this is where to practise it. ByteBook records the purchases and sales; the closing stock value is a calculation you make and keep with the working papers.

chapterTitle: Closing a month and a year
title: Leases, if the business rents premises or equipment
text: A contract is, or contains, a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration NZ IFRS 16.9. At the commencement date the lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability NZ IFRS 16.22. In plain words: a long lease is recognised in the balance sheet, not simply expensed as rent. Short-term and low-value leases have practical exemptions, which is why the rent line in a small business is a mix of both treatments.

chapterTitle: Closing a month and a year
title: Events after the reporting date
text: Work does not stop on balance date. The standard divides the time afterwards into two kinds of event, and the treatment differs: Adjusting events provide evidence of conditions that existed at the reporting date. The amounts in the financial statements are adjusted to reflect them NZ IAS 10.8. A customer who owed $40,000 going into liquidation shortly after balance date is the classic example: the customer was already in trouble at the date. Non-adjusting events concern conditions that arose after the reporting date. The amounts are not adjusted, but a material event may still need to be disclosed NZ IAS 10.10. An auditor performs procedures designed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about events between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report ISA 560.6. After the report is signed, the auditor has no obligation to keep looking — but if a fact comes to light before the statements are issued, the standard says what to do about it ISA 560.10.

chapterTitle: Closing a month and a year
title: Going concern
text: One question sits underneath all of this. Are these financial statements prepared on the basis that the business will keep trading? The objective of the auditor is to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about, and conclude on, the appropriateness of management's use of the going concern basis of accounting ISA 570.9. Where management has not yet made an assessment, the auditor asks them to make one ISA 570.16. For the person doing the books, the practical version is this: if the business cannot pay its debts as they fall due, the accounts look different, and the time to raise it is during the closing routine rather than after the statements are issued. :::check 1.
