A customer owing $40,000 at balance date is placed in liquidation three weeks later. Adjusting or non-adjusting, and why? 3. Stock that cost $8,000 will now sell for $5,500 net of selling costs. What is the effect on the financial statements? :::

chapterTitle: Nothing is deleted: voiding, not editing
title: The temptation
text: You post an invoice to the wrong customer. Or an amount is typed as $1,290 instead of $1,209. The tidy thing is to fix it: change the number, and the books look as though the mistake never happened. That is exactly the habit this chapter is here to break.

chapterTitle: Nothing is deleted: voiding, not editing
title: What ByteBook does instead
text: No posted entry in the books is deleted or edited in place. A mistake is voided . Voiding marks the original entry as void and posts the mirror image of it: the same accounts, the same amounts, the opposite direction. Both stay in the books and both are still counted, so they cancel each other out in every total. The figures end up where they should have been, and the record shows both what happened and what was done about it. Drafts are different: a draft is not in the books yet, so it can be changed or deleted. Bank lines that have not been coded can be removed from the statement, and ordinary names, accounts and settings can be edited. The rule is about posted entries, which are the record. Three consequences follow, and each is worth knowing: 1. The net effect is correct. The books are not wrong because a mistake was made and corrected. They are wrong only if the mistake is still uncorrected. 2. The history is intact. Anyone can see that an entry was raised in error, on what date, and what was done. 3. The fingerprint chain still holds. A voided entry keeps the fingerprint it was sealed with, so voiding does not break the chain that chapter 12 describes. Editing the original wo

chapterTitle: Nothing is deleted: voiding, not editing
title: What this has to do with auditing
text: An auditor's working papers have to do a specific job: they must allow another auditor, who has never seen the engagement, to understand what was done. The auditing standard puts it plainly. The auditor shall prepare audit documentation that is sufficient to enable an experienced auditor, having no previous connection with the audit, to understand the nature, timing and extent of the procedures performed, the results, and the significant matters and judgements ISA 230.8. Now read that against the two habits: Habit What the next auditor can see --- --- Edit the entry A number that has changed, and no record of what it was Void and re-post The original, the correction, the dates, and the reason The second one is a working paper. The first one is a gap, and an unexplained gap in a set of books is worse than a visible mistake. The same discipline applies to the person doing the books. Documentation has to be prepared on a timely basis ISA 230.7 — which in practice means correcting an entry when you notice it, not at the end of the year when you have forgotten why.

chapterTitle: Nothing is deleted: voiding, not editing
title: How to void something in ByteBook
text: Open the document or the transaction, choose Void this document (or Void and reverse on a transaction), and write the reason. The reason is optional in the form, but write one: it is the part that matters six months later. If a payment has already been recorded, open the invoice first and choose Reverse the payment , then void. The entry and its mirror image remain in the books, the pair cancels out in the totals, and the audit trail records what happened.

chapterTitle: Nothing is deleted: voiding, not editing
title: A practical rule
text: Before you correct anything, ask what a new person would need to see in order to agree with your corrected figure. If the answer involves knowing something that is not written down, write it down. That is the whole of it. :::check 1. An invoice for $1,290 should have been $1,209. If the original is edited, what is lost? 2. Why does voiding not break the fingerprint chain? 3. What does ISA 230.8 require the documentation to make possible? :::

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: The idea
text: A bookkeeping record is a claim about the past, and the claim is only useful if you can tell whether it has been altered since it was written. ByteBook seals every entry with a SHA-256 fingerprint : a short string of characters computed from the entry's own contents — its date, its accounts, its amounts, its description. Change any of that and the fingerprint changes. There is no way to adjust an entry and keep the same fingerprint. Then it does the second, more useful thing. Each entry's fingerprint is computed including the fingerprint of the entry before it . This is a chain, and it has a property that a list of separate fingerprints does not: altering an entry anywhere in the middle breaks every fingerprint after it. To alter an old entry and leave no trace, you would have to recompute every entry that follows, in order, in secret. The books are a file on a disk, so that is not impossible — but it is no longer a quiet edit.

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: What the Audit trail page shows
text: Open Audit trail . ByteBook recomputes the whole chain from the recorded entries, including the voided entries whose fingerprints do not change when they are voided, and reports: how many entries there are; how many verify; how many links are broken, if any; a fingerprint of the whole ledger. If a link is broken, the page says so, and the meaning is specific: something wrote to the books outside ByteBook. That is not a bookkeeping error. It is a statement about the record itself, and it is worth more than a page of clean ticks.

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: The chain, drawn
text: The chain page shows the same thing at three scales, because one picture cannot answer both "is this intact?" and "what exactly is in this entry?". The ribbon is the whole record on a time axis. Each mark is one day, and how tall it is tells you how many entries that day holds. Under the marks runs the chain itself — a line that is solid where the links hold and broken where they do not. Under that, each sealed period is drawn as a span across the days it covers, linked to the period before it. Everything the record has ever held is in that ribbon: it is not sampled and it is not paginated. The chain below is the entries in order, each one a block and each fingerprint a line between two. The window starts at the most recent two dozen entries; click a day on the ribbon to open it, or press Everything to see the lot. Click a block to read the entry behind it, click a link to see the two hashes it joins. A correction is a block too: a voided entry stays in the picture, because it is part of the history. The panel beside them takes one entry apart. It shows what was hashed — the date, the reference, the description, the type, the accounts and the amounts — and the fingerprint that came

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: Proving one entry without the whole ledger
text: The chain and the tree answer two different questions, and it is worth keeping them apart. The chain asks has anything moved? To answer it you have to read every entry from the beginning, because each one is built on the one before. That is the right question for the owner of the books and the wrong one for somebody checking a single invoice. The Merkle tree asks was this entry in the ledger? The fingerprints of all the entries are folded together in pairs until one value is left, and that value is the Merkle root. To prove that one entry belongs, you need its fingerprint and one sibling hash per level: about ten hashes for a thousand entries, not a thousand. That is what Fetch the proof gives you, and what chapter 14 puts in the file an external auditor can check on their own computer.

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: Where this fits in an audit
text: The chain is not a replacement for an auditor's procedures, and ByteBook does not claim it is. It answers one narrow question extremely well: has the record changed since it was written? That question sits underneath several others. When an auditor relies on the books, they are relying on the information in them being relevant and reliable ISA 500.7. A chain of fingerprints is evidence about reliability that is produced by the system itself, on every entry, rather than sampled. Procedure A01 in chapter 13 reports it as part of the routine: entries verified, broken links, and the fingerprint of the whole ledger. Procedure A12 then asks the next question: does a period that was sealed still match the ledger as it stands now? :::aside What the chain does not prove It does not prove that the entries are correct. A perfectly intact chain of entries posted to the wrong account is still a set of books with the wrong numbers in it. The chain proves integrity, not accuracy, and the two are different claims. An auditor needs both. :::

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: What catches what
text: Five things can happen to a record, and they are not caught by the same thing. Knowing which is which is most of what makes the rest of this part useful. If somebody… What catches it --- --- changes a figure in an old entry the entry's own fingerprint: the block turns red deletes an entry from the middle the link the next entry carries posts into a period that was already sealed procedure A09, and the pack itself rewrites the whole record, end to end a receipt held outside the file enters a figure that is simply wrong a person The fourth line is the one people find surprising, and it is worth being exact about. Somebody with the file, the algorithm and the patience can recompute every fingerprint and leave a chain that verifies perfectly. Nothing inside the file can detect that, because there is nothing inside the file that disagrees. A copy of the fingerprints held somewhere else can, which is what a checkpoint receipt is for. See chapter 14.

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: What to do when a link breaks
text: 1. Stop and find out what wrote to the file. Restore, tooling, a script, a copy edited by hand — a broken chain always has a cause, and the cause is the finding. 2. Do not re-seal anything. Recomputing fingerprints to make a broken chain look intact destroys the only evidence you have. 3. Record what you found. In a training exercise, that note is the answer.

chapterTitle: The audit trail and the chain
title: What gets hashed, exactly
text: It is worth reading once, because it is where a chain either holds or leaks. The fingerprint of an entry is computed from this text and nothing else: Voiding an entry afterwards does not change its fingerprint. That is deliberate: voiding is a legitimate correction, and a correction that broke the chain it sits in would make the chain useless. The reversal is posted beside the original, and both stay in the chain. Two consequences follow, and both are worth knowing before somebody asks. What the fingerprint covers: the money, and the words that identify the entry. A change to any of those is caught, on that entry and on every entry after it. What it does not cover: the tax code on a line, the contact, and the line description. Those can change without breaking the chain. A chain that verifies is therefore proof that the amounts and the entry itself are as they were written, and not proof that the GST treatment is the one somebody typed. That gap is why the tree exists. Its leaf for an entry is a fingerprint of every field the entry holds — the tax codes, the contacts and the line descriptions included — written as JSON with sorted keys so it cannot be rearranged into a different en

chapterTitle: The sixteen assurance procedures
title: What this screen is
text: Open Assurance . Sixteen procedures run on every visit, against the actual entries in the books. Each one has a reference, a title, an objective, and a result. Each one offers a working paper you can download as a CSV. The page says something important about itself. These procedures report what they found and leave the conclusion to you. It does not say "the records are wrong". It says "three documents are missing a GST number". The difference between those two statements is the difference between a procedure and a conclusion, and it is the thing this chapter is really about.

chapterTitle: The sixteen assurance procedures
title: The programme
text: Ref Procedure The objective, in the program's own words --- --- --- A01 Ledger integrity Every entry still carries the fingerprint it was sealed with, and each one includes the fingerprint of the entry before it A02 Double entry Every transaction moves money from somewhere to somewhere else: the two sides of each entry must be equal A03 Bank reconciliation The bank balance in the ledger agrees with the balance on the statement, and every imported line has been dealt with A04 Debtors Money owed to the business is real, correctly aged, and not overpaid A05 Creditors Money the business owes is recorded, and no bill is paid twice A06 GST reconciliation The GST in the return is the GST in the ledger, and the control accounts agree with what has been filed A07 Journal entries Entries that did not come from an invoice, a bill or the bank are where adjustments hide A08 Duplicate payments The same amount, described the same way, twice within a week is usually a mistake, and sometimes a fraud A09 Cut-off Entries dated in the future, or inside a period that has already been packed and closed, are the two ways a figure moves after the fact A10 Documents and compliance A tax invoice over $50 ha

chapterTitle: The sixteen assurance procedures
title: Reading a result
text: Each procedure ends in one of three states, and the distinction is deliberate. No exceptions. The procedure ran and found nothing to report. Exceptions to look at (the page counts them). The procedure found something specific: four bank lines not coded, three documents missing a GST number, three figures that do not reproduce from the ledger. For information. Nothing is wrong; the procedure is telling you something you should know. Three manual entries exist. Nothing has been sealed yet. The page sorts exceptions to the top, then information, then clean results, so the first thing you read is the thing that needs a decision.

chapterTitle: The sixteen assurance procedures
title: Six procedures worth understanding properly
text: A07, journal entries. A journal is an entry that came from nowhere: not an invoice, not a bill, not the bank. Most journals are perfectly ordinary — depreciation, an accrual, a correction. But because they are not tied to a document, they are also the natural place to put a figure that has no support. An auditor's response is not suspicion, it is a question: what is the paperwork behind this one, and who posted it? The procedure lists every manual entry with who posted it and when, so the question can be asked precisely. A08, duplicate payments. The same amount described the same way twice inside a week is usually a mistake and occasionally a fraud. Either way it is worth the two minutes it takes to check against the supplier's statement. A09, cut-off. Two patterns, and both matter. An entry dated in the future has been posted into a period that has not happened. An entry dated inside a period that was already sealed and closed has changed a figure after the fact. Neither is automatically wrong; both need an explanation before anyone relies on the period. A14, reproduce the numbers. This is the check that catches a reporting bug rather than a bookkeeping error. The reports are reca

chapterTitle: The sixteen assurance procedures
title: Why fraud gets its own thinking
text: Four of the sixteen procedures are aimed at fraud rather than error, and the reason is in the auditing standards. When the auditor identifies and assesses the risks of material misstatement due to fraud, there is a presumption that there are risks of fraud in revenue recognition, and the auditor has to evaluate which types of revenue, revenue transactions or assertions give rise to those risks ISA 240.27. The second is about who is best placed to do it. Management is in a unique position to perpetrate fraud, because of the ability to manipulate accounting records and override controls that otherwise appear to be working ISA 240.32. That is why journal entries and unusual transactions get attention even when everything else looks well controlled.

chapterTitle: The sixteen assurance procedures
title: Professional scepticism
text: The quality of every procedure on this page depends on one habit, and it has a name. When applying the conceptual framework in the ethics standard, an assurance practitioner is required to have an enquiring mind, exercise professional judgement, and apply the reasonable and informed third party test PES 1 R120.5. An enquiring mind is not suspicion. It is the willingness to ask what the evidence actually supports, rather than what you expect it to show. The exception list on this page is where that habit starts: something is different from what you expected, and the next step is to find out why. :::check 1. Why does the page distinguish "exceptions to look at" from "for information"? 2. Which procedure would catch a figure that was changed after a period was closed, and how? 3. A procedure reports four exceptions. Has the auditor reached a conclusion? Explain. :::

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: Sealing a period
text: Fingerprints protect entries one at a time. A sealed pack protects a whole period at once. When you seal a period, ByteBook takes its entries, its figures, the fingerprint of the whole ledger, and the fingerprint of the pack before it, and hashes them together into one value. That value is the pack's fingerprint. Verifying a pack recomputes it from the ledger as it stands now. The consequence is sharp and easy to demonstrate: Backdate an entry into a sealed period and the pack's fingerprint changes. Verification fails, and it fails because of the change , not because something is missing. Void an entry inside a sealed period and the same thing happens — correctly, because the period's totals moved, and moving them after the fact is precisely what a sealed pack is designed to detect. Linking each pack to the one before it means the periods form a chain of their own, one level up from the entries.

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: Timeline: what a pack protects
text: 1. Work the period. Invoice, code the bank, file GST. 2. Check it. Run the assurance procedures; deal with what they found. 3. Seal it. Open Audit trail → Sealed packs , choose the period and press Seal this period . ByteBook records the pack and its fingerprint. 4. Later, verify it. Reopen the pack and check it. The fingerprint is recomputed from the entries as they are now. Match or no match, with no discretion in between. 5. If it fails, find out why. In a training exercise the cause is usually a backdated entry, and finding it is the exercise.

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: Working papers
text: Every procedure offers a working paper as a CSV. That is the format an auditor actually wants: a table you can open, check, and attach to a file, with the columns named and the figures traceable. Two things make a working paper useful, and both are about the reader rather than the writer: It says what was done. Not "bank checked", but the balance in the ledger, the balance on the statement, the difference, and the date. It says what it found. Four exceptions, listed, so that a second person can re-perform the check and get the same answer. This is ISA 230.8 applied to a small business: documentation sufficient for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the engagement to understand what was done, what the results were, and what was concluded.

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: Assembling the file
text: There is a finishing step, and it has a deadline. The auditor assembles the documentation into an audit file and completes the administrative process of assembling the final audit file on a timely basis after the date of the auditor's report ISA 230.14. Where there is a legal or regulatory deadline to complete the assembly, the standard's own period applies. In ByteBook the equivalent is short: run the procedures, download the working papers (the CSV button on each procedure), seal the period, record a checkpoint ( Audit trail → Checkpoints → Check the record now ), take a backup, and put the pack's fingerprint in the file. The fingerprint is one line, and it is what lets a reader verify the period years later without re-reading everything.

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: Handing the record to somebody outside
text: An external auditor is usually given a PDF and a set of CSVs, and then has to take the numbers on trust. Audit trail → Hand it over produces the alternative: one folder, or one zip, containing the record itself and a small checker that tests it. In the training exercises, the same checks are on the Audit trail and The chain pages; running verify.py is the receiving auditor's job, not the learner's. In the bundle What it is --- --- entries.csv one row per entry, with the fingerprint it carries lines.csv one row per journal line, which is what the fingerprint covers packs.json every sealed period, with the figures it sealed checkpoints.json what the record looked like each time it was witnessed receipts/ one receipt per checkpoint, to keep or pass on manifest.json what is inside, and a fingerprint of every file verify.py the script that checks all of the above README.txt what the folder is, in words The auditor unpacks the folder and runs one small checker, verify.py (a reader who wants to repeat the checks inside ByteBook can use Audit trail → The chain → Fetch the proof instead): Python is a free program; if it is installed, that is all the checker needs. No ByteBook, no internet,

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: A read-only key, for an internal auditor
text: An external auditor usually wants a file. An internal auditor, or the organisation's own scripts, may want to pull the figures repeatedly and test them with their own tools. That is what an audit key is for: a named, revocable, read-only credential for the audit API. The whole surface is twelve GET endpoints, all of which show what the pages show: /verify — is the chain intact, and the Merkle root /entries , /lines — the rows, as JSON or CSV /proof/{id} — one entry, proved against the whole ledger /packs , /checkpoints — what was sealed and what was witnessed /procedures , /working-paper/{code} — the programme and its papers /bundle — the whole folder, as a zip /tokens , /access-log — which keys exist, and who read what, including the attempts that were refused /help — the list itself, for a tool that wants to discover it Four properties make this something an organisation can actually hand out. 1. A key cannot write. It cannot post, edit, void, seal, or change a setting. It is refused in the language it asked in — JSON, with a reason — rather than being quietly redirected. 2. A key is shown once. Only its SHA-256 is kept, so a copy of the database does not hand anybody a working k

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: A checkpoint, and why a receipt matters
text: A checkpoint is one line of evidence. Every time somebody checks the record — or seals a period, which does the same thing by itself — ByteBook writes down how many entries there were, the fingerprint of the last one, and the Merkle root of the whole ledger. Each checkpoint includes the fingerprint of the checkpoint before it, so the log of checks is a chain of its own. On its own that is still just another table in the same file. It becomes evidence when a copy leaves the file, and that copy is a receipt : two dozen lines with the business name, the date, the entry count, the last fingerprint, the Merkle root and the checkpoint's own fingerprint. Keep a receipt the way you would keep a bank statement. Email it to your accountant at every month end, print it, drop it in the audit file. It costs nothing. What it buys is this: a record rewritten as a whole can rebuild every entry fingerprint, but it cannot reach the copy in somebody else's inbox. To check one, paste it into Audit trail → Checkpoints → Check a receipt . The printed version and the JSON version both work. ByteBook says whether the books still contain everything the receipt witnessed, and how much work has happened sinc

chapterTitle: Sealed packs and working papers
title: What stays outside the program
text: ByteBook can prove that a period has not changed, that the two sides of every entry are equal, that the bank agrees, and that the figures on the reports can be reproduced from the rows. Those are arithmetic and record-integrity claims, and a computer is good at them. It cannot judge whether a debt will be collected, whether a provision is adequate, whether a related party transaction was on arm's length terms, or whether a business is a going concern. Those are judgements, and they come with a person's name attached. Knowing which side of that line you are standing on is most of what makes an auditor useful. :::check 1. An entry is backdated into a period that was sealed last month. What fails, and when is it detected? 2. Why does a void inside a sealed period fail the verification, when the void is a legitimate correction? 3. Name two claims ByteBook can test and two it cannot. 4. An auditor is given a bundle and the checker prints PASS. Name three things that does not tell them. 5. Why does keeping a receipt matter more than recording a checkpoint? :::

chapterTitle: Roles: who may do what
title: The four roles
text: Role May do --- --- Owner Everything, including settings, backups and who can sign in General manager Run the books: invoices, bills, bank, GST, reports Accountant Read everything, including the tax working papers; change nothing Auditor Read the books and the assurance work; no settings, change nothing Two of those roles cannot change a number, and that is the feature.

chapterTitle: Roles: who may do what
title: The rule that keeps it honest
text: ByteBook will not switch on another person's sign-in until the owner has set a password of their own, and the security settings open only for the owner. That single rule prevents the obvious failure: nobody can hand out a login that locks the owner out of their own books. It also means every role was created deliberately, from the owner's own screen. ByteBook does not keep a separate log of role changes, so in a training business write down who set it up and when.

chapterTitle: Roles: who may do what
title: Why an auditor should not be able to edit
text: The ethics standard states the requirement plainly. An assurance practitioner shall comply with the principle of objectivity, which requires exercising judgement without being compromised by bias, a conflict of interest, or undue influence PES 1 R112.1. An assurance practitioner shall also comply with the principle of integrity, which requires being straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships PES 1 R111.1, and with professional competence and due care PES 1 R113.1. An auditor who holds the ability to change the records they are auditing is in a position where objectivity cannot be demonstrated, however honest they are. The read-only role removes the question rather than asking anyone to be trusted about it. The same logic runs through the whole quality management system in a firm. The objective of that system is to provide the firm with reasonable assurance that the firm and its personnel fulfil their responsibilities and perform engagements in accordance with professional standards PES 3.14. Access control is a small, concrete piece of the same idea.

chapterTitle: Roles: who may do what
title: Access is also an assurance question
text: ByteBook's A13 procedure reports who can sign in, when the books were last backed up, and whether anything failed quietly while people were working. It is the least glamorous procedure of the sixteen and one of the most useful, because the questions it asks are exactly the ones an engagement team asks about any system they are relying on: who has access, is the record protected, and would anybody have noticed if something went wrong.

chapterTitle: Roles: who may do what
title: A practical training routine
text: When you work through the Marine Parade Dental practice business, which is the one meant to be audited: 1. Set the owner password first. 2. Add an accountant login and use it to prepare the tax figures. 3. Add an auditor login and run the assurance procedures from it. 4. Try to change something as the auditor. Notice that you cannot, and that the program does not offer you the option. 5. Switch back to the owner and void something deliberately. Then look at the audit trail as the auditor and find it. Step five is the exercise that makes the rest of the design make sense. :::check 1. Why does adding another user require the owner's password? 2. Which standard principle is behind giving an auditor a read-only login? 3. What does procedure A13 report, and why does it belong in an assurance programme at all? :::

chapterTitle: How to read a standard reference
title: Two families of document
text: Everything this handbook refers to comes from one of two families. Accounting standards say how a transaction is recognised, measured and disclosed, and what the financial statements must show. In New Zealand they are the NZ IFRS standards, issued by the External Reporting Board. Each one carries an international standard from the International Accounting Standards Board with New Zealand additions, which is why they are called NZ IAS 1, NZ IFRS 15, and so on. Auditing and assurance standards say how the work of checking those financial statements is planned, performed, documented and reported. In New Zealand they are the ISAs (NZ) , issued within the External Reporting Board, alongside the PES standards for ethics, quality management and engagement quality reviews. Each ISA (NZ) carries an international standard from the IAASB with New Zealand additions.

chapterTitle: How to read a standard reference
title: Reading an identifier
text: The identifier is the shorthand a working paper uses. Take NZ IAS 1.15 : Part Means --- --- NZ IAS 1 The New Zealand standard: NZ IAS 1, Presentation of Financial Statements .15 Paragraph 15 of that standard And ISA (NZ) 230.8 : Part Means --- --- ISA (NZ) 230 The New Zealand auditing standard: ISA (NZ) 230, Audit Documentation .8 Paragraph 8 The naming carries history you will meet constantly: IAS numbering is old — standards issued before the International Accounting Standards Board was formed in 2001, and still in force. IAS 1, IAS 2, IAS 7. IFRS numbering came after. IFRS 9, IFRS 15, IFRS 16. IFRIC and SIC are interpretations: short documents that settle how a standard applies to a particular situation. FRS is used for New Zealand domestic standards that have no international equivalent. (Revised) in an auditing standard's name means it has been rewritten. ISA (NZ) 315 changed substantially in 2019, and ISA (NZ) 570 was revised in 2024. Citing the superseded version is a real and common error.

chapterTitle: How to read a standard reference
title: Why paragraph numbers matter
text: A reference to "the standard on going concern" is not checkable. A reference to paragraph 16 of ISA (NZ) 570 is: it says one specific thing, and a reader can find it in a minute. For the audit side this matters even more than for accounting. An auditor's working paper cites paragraphs, because the whole point of the paper is that somebody else can re-perform the reasoning.

chapterTitle: How to read a standard reference
title: Effective dates
text: Every standard here has a date from which it applies, usually expressed as periods beginning on or after a certain date. Two standards on the same subject can both exist while the older one still applies to an earlier period. The library records, for each standard, the effective date as the publisher states it, plus the date the document was issued and the date it was compiled to. When you quote a standard, check all three. A version compiled in one year may carry the same number as a version compiled a decade later and say something different.

chapterTitle: How to read a standard reference
title: Following a reference to its source
text: Every citation in this handbook can be followed. Each one gives you: the identifier, so you can search for it; the publisher — the XRB for New Zealand standards, IFAC for the IAASB Handbook; the address of the document on the publisher's own site; the SHA-256 of the copy this handbook was checked against. The last item is what makes the reference checkable rather than merely pointed at. If the publisher later issues a new version, the fingerprint in this handbook will no longer match the document at that address — which is exactly the signal that says go and read the new one .

chapterTitle: How to read a standard reference
title: The limits of a reference
text: Quoting a paragraph is not applying it. A paragraph tells you what the standard requires; it does not tell you whether your contract is a lease, whether your revenue is recognised over time or at a point in time, or whether a debt will be collected. Those are judgements made on facts, and the standard is the frame you make them in. This handbook tries to keep the two apart on every page: the fact, then the judgement, then the reference that constrains the judgement. :::check 1. What does the (NZ) in ISA (NZ) 230 tell you about that document? 2. Why is ISA (NZ) 315.28 a better working paper reference than "the risk assessment standard"? 3. What does a changed SHA-256 for a standard tell you, and what should you do about it? :::

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
text: This chapter is a map, not a substitute. Each entry gives the question the standard answers, the requirements you will meet in these exercises, and where to see it happen.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 1 — Presentation of Financial Statements
text: The question: what must a set of financial statements contain, and what does it mean to present them fairly? A complete set includes a statement of financial position, a statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, a statement of changes in equity, a statement of cash flows, and notes NZ IAS 1.10. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events and conditions NZ IAS 1.15. Where an entity departs from a requirement to achieve a fair presentation, the departure and its effect are disclosed. The statement of financial position presents specified line items where they are relevant NZ IAS 1.54. The profit or loss section presents specified line items in addition to those required by other standards NZ IAS 1.82. Expenses are analysed by nature or by function, whichever provides reliable and more relevant information NZ IAS 1.99. Accounting policy information is disclosed where it is material NZ IAS 1.117, along with the judgements management made in applying those policies NZ IAS 1.122 and the major sources of estimation uncertainty NZ IAS 1.125. In ByteBook: Reports → Balance sheet and Profit and loss. The balance sheet

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 7 — Statement of Cash Flows
text: The question: where did the money come from, and where did it go? Cash flows are classified as operating, investing or financing activities NZ IAS 7.10. Operating cash flows are presented by the direct method, showing gross receipts and payments, or by the indirect method, starting from profit NZ IAS 7.18. Investing and financing transactions that do not use cash at all are excluded from the statement and disclosed elsewhere NZ IAS 7.43. In ByteBook: Reports → Money in and out.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 8 — Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors
text: The question: what happens when a number you reported last year turns out to have been wrong? A change in an accounting estimate is recognised prospectively, in this period and future ones NZ IAS 8.36. A material prior period error is corrected retrospectively NZ IAS 8.42. In ByteBook: the void and correct routine in chapter 11. A correction that reverses a wrong figure is visible in the audit trail, which is what makes the treatment checkable.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 10 — Events after the Reporting Period
text: The question: the balance date has passed and something has happened. Does it change the accounts? Adjusting events provide evidence of conditions that existed at the reporting date, and the amounts recognised are adjusted NZ IAS 10.8. Non-adjusting events concern conditions that arose after the reporting date. The amounts are not adjusted NZ IAS 10.10, though material ones may need disclosure. In ByteBook: the closing routine in chapter 10, and the cut-off procedure A09.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IFRS 9 — Financial Instruments
text: The question: how much of the money customers owe will actually be paid? For trade receivables, the loss allowance is measured at an amount equal to lifetime expected credit losses NZ IFRS 9 5.5.15. In ByteBook: Reports → Who owes what, and the debtors procedure A04.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IFRS 15 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers
text: The question: when has a business earned its revenue? Revenue is recognised when the entity satisfies a performance obligation by transferring a promised good or service to the customer NZ IFRS 15.31. Where a performance obligation is not satisfied over time, it is satisfied at a point in time NZ IFRS 15.38. When a performance obligation is satisfied, revenue is the amount of the transaction price allocated to it NZ IFRS 15.46. The transaction price is allocated to the performance obligations on a relative stand-alone selling price basis NZ IFRS 15.73. In ByteBook: Invoices, and the builder's stage payments.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IFRS 16 — Leases
text: The question: is this rental an expense, or an asset and a liability? A contract is, or contains, a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration NZ IFRS 16.9. At the commencement date the lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability NZ IFRS 16.22. In ByteBook: the recurring rent entries post rent as an ordinary expense. ByteBook does not do lease accounting; a long lease would need a manual journal for the right-of-use asset and the lease liability, outside these exercises.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 16 — Property, Plant and Equipment
text: The question: when is a purchase an expense, and when is it something the business owns? An item that qualifies for recognition is measured at its cost NZ IAS 16.15. The depreciable amount is allocated on a systematic basis over the useful life NZ IAS 16.50. Depreciation begins when the asset is available for use NZ IAS 16.55. In ByteBook: the expenses procedure A11, which reports the large one-off costs where this question has to be asked.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 2 — Inventories
text: The question: what is the stock worth on the balance sheet? Inventories are measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value NZ IAS 2.9. Cost comprises the costs of purchase, the costs of conversion, and the other costs of bringing the inventories to their present location and condition NZ IAS 2.10. Cost is assigned using first-in, first-out or a weighted average cost formula NZ IAS 2.25. Where cost is not recoverable, the write-down is recognised as an expense in the period it happens NZ IAS 2.28. In ByteBook: the Pacific Trading practice business. ByteBook records the purchases and sales; it does not keep a stock ledger, so the closing valuation is a calculation the learner makes and keeps with the working papers.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 37 — Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
text: The question: when do you put a cost in the accounts for something that has not happened yet? A provision is recognised where there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow of resources is probable, and a reliable estimate can be made NZ IAS 37.14. The amount recognised is the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the obligation at the reporting date NZ IAS 37.36. In ByteBook: the closing routine in chapter 10.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: NZ IAS 21 and NZ IAS 12
text: Two more you will meet as soon as a business trades across a border or has a tax bill. A foreign currency transaction is recorded by applying the spot exchange rate at the date of the transaction NZ IAS 21.21. Where the presentation currency differs from the functional currency, the results are translated for presentation NZ IAS 21.38. Current tax for the current and prior periods is measured at the amount expected to be paid to, or recovered from, the taxation authorities, using the tax rates and laws enacted or substantively enacted by the reporting date NZ IAS 12.46. In ByteBook: Reports → IRD working papers, which build the IR3, IR10 and IR4 from the same ledger.

chapterTitle: Accounting standards you will meet in these books
title: Two things this chapter does not cover
text: The framework for smaller entities. New Zealand has reporting tiers, set by XRB A1 and XRB A2. A business reporting under a reduced disclosure regime applies the same recognition and measurement rules with fewer disclosures, so the standard you reach for is the same and the disclosure requirements are not. Estimates that need a specialist. NZ IAS 36 impairment, NZ IAS 19 employee benefits and NZ IFRS 17 insurance contracts are all in the library and all outside the scope of a small-business set of books. They are named here so that you know what you have not read.

chapterTitle: Auditing standards you will meet in these procedures
title: Where an audit starts
text: The overall objectives of the auditor are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and then to report in accordance with the auditor's findings ISA 200.11. Everything below is machinery in service of that sentence. Notice what it promises and what it does not: reasonable assurance, not certainty, and about matters that are material, not about everything.

chapterTitle: Auditing standards you will meet in these procedures
title: Planning and risk
text: ISA (NZ) 300 — Planning. In establishing the overall audit strategy, the auditor considers the characteristics of the engagement that define its scope and the reporting objectives, among other things ISA 300.8. ISA (NZ) 315 — Risk assessment. The auditor has to understand the entity's information system relevant to the preparation of the financial statements ISA 315.25, and then identify the risks of material misstatement and determine whether they exist at the financial statement level or at the assertion level for classes of transactions, account balances and disclosures ISA 315.28. That last distinction is the one to carry away. "The receivables balance may be overstated" is an assertion-level risk. "The finance team is new and the systems changed" is a risk at the financial statement level. ISA (NZ) 320 — Materiality. The auditor determines materiality for the financial statements as a whole ISA 320.10, and performance materiality — a lower figure, set to reduce to an acceptably low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements exceed materiality ISA 320.11. ISA (NZ) 540 — Estimates and ISA (NZ) 550 — Related parties each need their own thinking. For relat

chapterTitle: Auditing standards you will meet in these procedures
title: Gathering evidence
text: ISA (NZ) 500 — Audit evidence. The auditor designs and performs audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances for the purpose of obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence ISA 500.6, and considers the relevance and reliability of the information to be used as evidence ISA 500.7. Sufficient is about quantity; appropriate is about relevance and reliability. ISA (NZ) 505 — External confirmations. Where the auditor identifies factors giving rise to doubts about the reliability of a response to a confirmation request, the auditor obtains further audit evidence to resolve those doubts ISA 505.10. ISA (NZ) 520 — Analytical procedures. Where substantive analytical procedures are used, the standard sets out what that involves, including determining the suitability of the data and evaluating whether the expectation is precise enough ISA 520.5. ISA (NZ) 330 — Responding to assessed risks. Further audit procedures are designed and performed so that their nature, timing and extent are responsive to the assessed risks at the assertion level ISA 330.6, and irrespective of those risks, substantive procedures are performed for each material class of transactions, account balance a

chapterTitle: Auditing standards you will meet in these procedures
title: Documenting the work
text: ISA (NZ) 230 — Audit documentation. Documentation is prepared on a timely basis ISA 230.7 and must be sufficient to enable an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit to understand the procedures performed and their results, the evidence obtained, and the significant matters, conclusions and judgements ISA 230.8. The final audit file is assembled on a timely basis after the date of the auditor's report ISA 230.14. This is the standard behind ByteBook's working papers and sealed packs. If you remember one auditing standard from this handbook, remember this one: it is the standard that makes every other procedure checkable.

chapterTitle: Auditing standards you will meet in these procedures
title: Communicating
text: ISA (NZ) 260 — Those charged with governance. The auditor communicates with the people responsible for overseeing the entity, which in a small company usually means the board or the owners. ISA (NZ) 265 — Deficiencies in internal control. Where deficiencies have been identified, the auditor determines whether, individually or in combination, they constitute significant deficiencies ISA 265.8. Notice the framing: the deficiency is reported, and the determination of significance is a judgement to be made and recorded.

chapterTitle: Auditing standards you will meet in these procedures
title: Fraud and subsequent events
text: ISA (NZ) 240 — Fraud. There is a presumption that there are risks of fraud in revenue recognition, and the auditor evaluates which types of revenue, revenue transactions or assertions give rise to those risks ISA 240.27. Management is in a unique position to perpetrate fraud because of the ability to manipulate accounting records and override controls that otherwise appear to be operating effectively ISA 240.32. ISA (NZ) 560 — Subsequent events. The auditor performs procedures designed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that all events occurring between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report that require adjustment or disclosure have been identified ISA 560.6.

chapterTitle: Auditing standards you will meet in these procedures
title: Going concern, representations and the opinion
text: ISA (NZ) 570 — Going concern. The objectives include obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence about, and concluding on, the appropriateness of management's use of the going concern basis of accounting ISA 570.9. Where management has not yet performed an assessment, the auditor requests that they make one ISA 570.16. ISA (NZ) 580 — Written representations. The auditor requests a written representation that management has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework ISA 580.10. A representation letter does not replace procedures; it is a formal record of who is responsible for what. ISA (NZ) 700 — The opinion. The auditor expresses an unmodified opinion when concluding that the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework ISA 700.16. Under a fair presentation framework, the opinion uses one of the phrases the standard specifies ISA 700.25. ISA (NZ) 701 — Key audit matters. title: Ethics and quality
text: PES 1 — International Code of Ethics for Assurance Practitioners (including International Independence Standards) (New Zealand). chapterTitle: Screen by screen: which standards apply where
title: How to use it
text: Three ways, depending on what you are doing. When you are learning a screen. Read the row before you start. Knowing that the bank reconciliation is tied to the standard on external confirmations changes how you read the page: you stop looking for a balance that agrees and start looking for evidence that comes from outside the business. When something looks wrong. Find the row, open the standard, and read the paragraph. The standard usually tells you what the correct treatment is and, just as often, what it is not. When you are writing a working paper. Cite the paragraph. Not the standard's name, not the general topic: the paragraph. A reference that cannot be checked is not a reference.

chapterTitle: Screen by screen: which standards apply where
title: A worked example: a bank line coded as an expense
text: Suppose the bank statement shows $1,150 paid to a supplier, and you code it to expenses when it should have been a payment against a bill. 1. What is wrong? The supplier's balance still shows as unpaid, and an expense has been recorded twice: once when the bill was entered, and again from the bank line. 2. Which accounting question is it? Whether the expense is recognised at the right amount in the right period — a matter of faithful representation NZ IAS 1.15. 3. Which procedure catches it? A05, creditors, which reports money the business owes and checks for a bill paid twice. The GST figures move as well, which A06 will see. 4. Which auditing standard applies? The reliability of the bank statement as evidence ISA 500.7, and the requirement that misstatements found during the audit are accumulated and communicated ISA 450.8. 5. How is it fixed? Open the coding entry under Transactions and choose Void and reverse . Then record the payment against the bill, from the bill itself, so the payment and the bill stay linked. Both the wrong entry and the correction stay in the record, and ISA 230.8 explains why that matters. That five-step shape — what is wrong, which accounting question,

chapterTitle: How this handbook stays accurate
title: The problem with a handbook
text: Any document that quotes standards is out of date the moment a standard changes, and it is most dangerous when it is confidently out of date. A handbook that teaches last year's rule with this year's certainty is worse than no handbook. So accuracy here is not a promise. It is a set of checks that run every time the handbook is published.

chapterTitle: How this handbook stays accurate
title: Where the documents come from
text: Every reference in this handbook points to a document that was downloaded from its publisher, stored, and fingerprinted: Publisher What they publish What we hold --- --- --- External Reporting Board (XRB) New Zealand accounting standards (NZ IFRS, which carry the IASB's text) and auditing standards (ISAs (NZ), PES and the framework) The current version of each standard, with its effective date and the address of the publisher's page IAASB, published by IFAC The Handbook of International Quality Management, Auditing, Review, Other Assurance, and Related Services Pronouncements , 2025 edition Volumes 1, 4 and 5, which carry the ISAs, the ISQMs, the assurance and review standards, and the framework Both publishers make these documents available free of charge. Neither permits their standards to be republished in full, which is why this handbook quotes short passages with attribution and links to the source rather than reproducing the text.

chapterTitle: How this handbook stays accurate
title: What is checked, and how
text: Three checks run over the handbook before it is published. Every reference must exist. A citation naming a standard that is not in the stored list stops publication. There is no path where a typo becomes a published reference to a standard that does not exist. Every cited paragraph must exist in the publisher's own text. The check reads the extracted text of the document, finds the paragraph by the number the citation gives, and shows the opening words of that paragraph. Where the paragraph cannot be found, publication fails: a reference cannot be published pointing at something that is not there. Every document must still have the fingerprint we recorded. Checking the stored documents fetches each one again and compares its SHA-256 (a unique fingerprint of the file's contents) with the one recorded when it was first downloaded. A difference means the publisher has issued a new version, and the handbook is re-checked against it before anything is republished. That third check is the one that keeps this honest over time. It cannot be argued with: either the bytes match or they do not.

chapterTitle: How this handbook stays accurate
title: What you can check yourself
text: Every citation in this handbook shows the identifier, the publisher, the address of the source document, and the fingerprint of the copy that was read. You do not need to check any of it to use the handbook; it is there so that a claim can be traced if somebody wants to. Follow the link, find the paragraph, and read it. If this handbook has misread a standard, that is how it will be found, and finding it is the point of the design.

chapterTitle: How this handbook stays accurate
title: When a standard changes
text: Standards change in three ways, and each is handled differently. A new version of an existing standard. A revised ISA (NZ) 315 or a recompiled NZ IAS 1 will show up as a changed fingerprint and a changed effective date. The references that touch it are reviewed, and the handbook states the new effective date. A new standard. NZ IFRS 18, Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements , takes effect for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027 and will change how performance is presented. It is already in the library, and it will appear in these pages as it becomes applicable. A withdrawal. A standard superseded by another stays in the library with the period it applied to, because a working paper about a 2023 audit still has to cite the 2023 rule.

chapterTitle: How this handbook stays accurate
title: A caution about dates
text: This edition states the effective date of each standard as the publisher gave it at the time of writing. Effective dates are the thing most likely to have moved. Before you rely on a reference for a live engagement, open the publisher's page from the citation and read the current version. That takes a minute and it is the only way to be certain. :::check 1. chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: How to run a session
text: Each session takes about an hour. The shape is the same every time: 1. Open the business in ByteBook: in the sidebar, under Set up , choose Practice businesses . The cards are labelled by trade; find the trade named in the session and press Start this business . 2. Do the task in the application. The task always ends with a document or a number somebody else could check. 3. Run the assurance procedures and write down what they found. 4. Mark it against the note at the end of the session. Marking is where the learning happens, so do not skip step four.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 1 — Bright Cuts (hairdressing, no GST)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Hairdressing (the books of Bright Cuts) → Start this business. Task: Raise three invoices, record two payments, and produce the profit and loss report for the quarter. Marking note: The business is not registered for GST, so no GST appears on any document, no GST return is expected, and the invoice totals equal the revenue. A candidate who records a GST figure has applied last week's habit instead of reading the settings. Look for evidence that they checked the registration status before invoicing.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 2 — Kōwhai Advisory (consulting, payments basis)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Consulting (the books of Kōwhai Advisory) → Start this business. Task: Work out the GST return for the quarter, then explain why the figure changes if you switch the period to include the following month. Marking note: The business files on the payments basis, so a March invoice paid in May belongs in the later period. The correct answer explains that the basis moves the transaction, not the invoice date. The most common wrong answer treats the invoice date as decisive.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 3 — Tasman Builders Ltd (construction, stage payments)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Construction (the books of Tasman Builders Ltd) → Start this business. Task: Explain, for one contract, why more than one invoice is raised, and what each invoice recognises. Marking note: Revenue is recognised as each performance obligation is satisfied NZ IFRS 15.31. Each stage invoice recognises the work transferred in that stage, not the whole contract at the first invoice and not on receipt of money. Look for the phrase as the work is done , and for a candidate who can say what would change if the whole contract were invoiced up front.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 4 — Harbour Cafe & Co (hospitality, volume)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Hospitality (the books of Harbour Cafe & Co) → Start this business. Task: Open the bank reconciliation. Read the ledger balance, the statement balance saved with the business and its date, and the difference. Explain what the page is testing, and what document a real reconciliation needs. Then explain how one lump deposit covers several trading days. Marking note: The first lesson is that a reconciliation is evidence only if the balance compared comes from an outside document — here the statement the business was built from — and that a saved balance has a date for a reason. The second is tying the money in the bank to the money rung up: every line accounted for, and an explanation in words of why a deposit and a day's takings are not the same number. Mark down an answer that only says "the balances match" without explaining either point.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 5 — Loom & Light (online retail, refunds)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Online retail (the books of Loom & Light) → Start this business. Task: Find the voided invoice and the reversal it produced, explain what each one did to revenue and GST, and then finish and post the draft invoice. Marking note: The reversal corrects the sale it belongs to. Revenue and GST both come back down, and the period it lands in is the period it happens. A candidate who treats the reversal as a new negative sale in a later period has the arithmetic right and the period wrong — and the GST reconciliation procedure will show it. The draft invoice is there to test whether "post" and "pay" are still understood as two separate events.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 6 — Marine Parade Rentals (residential property, exempt income)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Residential property (the books of Marine Parade Rentals) → Start this business. Task: Read the GST return for the period and explain why box 5 is larger than the taxable supplies suggest. Marking note: Exempt rent is income and is not taxable. Box 5 includes it; box 8 does not. The strongest answers note that GST on costs relating to exempt supplies is not claimable in the same way, which is the trap in this exercise and the reason the business is in the set.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 7 — Whirinaki Contracting (horticulture, six-monthly)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Horticulture (the books of Whirinaki Contracting) → Start this business. Task: Save the six-monthly return as a snapshot and reconcile it to the ledger. Marking note: A longer period contains more transactions and more chances for a misfiled one. The mark is for the reconciliation, not the total: the candidate should be able to show that the GST in the return is the GST in the ledger, transaction by transaction, rather than asserting that the totals match.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 8 — Foundry Labs (software, no revenue)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Software (the books of Foundry Labs) → Start this business. Task: Produce a balance sheet and a profit and loss report for a business with no income, and explain what each one says. Marking note: This is the session that separates people who can read reports from people who can produce them. With no revenue, the profit and loss report is all costs, and the balance sheet is where the money went. A strong answer explains that a growing loss with a falling bank balance and rising creditors describes a business being funded by someone, and names who.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 9 — Marine Parade Dental (health, security on)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Health (the books of Marine Parade Dental) → Start this business. Task: Switch security on, set up three roles, do a piece of bookkeeping as the general manager, and run the assurance procedures as the auditor. Marking note: The two things to look for are that the owner had set a password before any other sign-in could be switched on, and that the candidate noticed they could not change anything as the auditor. That second observation is the learning objective of the session.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 10 — Ngata Plumbing Ltd (trades, a busy statement)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Trades (the books of Ngata Plumbing Ltd) → Start this business. Task: Reconcile the bank, run the assurance procedures, and write a working-paper note on what the clean result does and does not prove. Then record the same manual payment twice — same amount, same description, same week — and show that A08 reports the pair. Marking note: Mark the explanations, not the exceptions. "The reconciliation agrees" is an observation. "The reconciliation agrees because every line is coded and the closing balance is the statement's balance at its date, so the bank is accounted for" is a finding. The deliberate duplicate is the second half: the candidate should be able to say which procedure noticed it (A08 looks for the same amount described the same way inside a week), why an honest pair can look like a duplicate, and what the correction must leave behind. Run Start over afterwards so the business is clean for the next person.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 11 — Pacific Trading Ltd (wholesale, inventory)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Wholesale (the books of Pacific Trading Ltd) → Start this business. Task: Read the balance sheet and the profit and loss for the year ended 30 June, find the bills to the overseas suppliers, and explain how the stock bought and sold shows up in those reports — then say how you would value the stock left on the shelves. Marking note: Inventories are measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value NZ IAS 2.9, and cost is assigned using first-in, first-out or a weighted average NZ IAS 2.25. ByteBook records the purchases and the sales; it does not keep a stock ledger, so the closing valuation is the candidate's own calculation and should show its working. The strongest answers say what they would do if the selling price fell: the write-down is recognised in the period it happens NZ IAS 2.28.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Session 12 — Precision Engineering Ltd (engineering, the rounding trap)
text: In the app: Practice businesses → Engineering (the books of Precision Engineering Ltd) → Start this business. Task: Open an invoice and multiply one line out by hand, then read what ByteBook stored. Find the bank line whose amount does not match the invoice it pays. Show, from the trial balance and A14, that the two sides agree to the cent and the reports reproduce from the rows. Marking note: This is the session that rewards patience. Money is handled as decimal cents, rounded half up, so a figure on a screen is the figure in the file. A candidate who finds a discrepancy should be able to say whether it came from a rounding rule, a GST split, or a miscoding — and should be able to show which entry caused it by reading the general ledger rather than the report.

chapterTitle: Twelve training sessions
title: Marking the whole course
text: Check What a pass looks like --- --- The numbers The reports are reproduced from the rows by procedure A14 The record No broken links in the chain; sealed periods verify The reasoning Every conclusion names the evidence behind it The references Every standard cited by paragraph, not by name The honesty Exceptions are reported with their cause, not hidden

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 1. What ByteBook is
text: 1. In one database file on the computer it runs on — ~/Library/Application Support/ByteBook/ on a Mac, %APPDATA%\ByteBook\ on Windows. A mistake is voided, not deleted: the original and its mirror image both stay in the record. 2. Any three of: a GST return built from the transactions; a bank reconciliation against an outside document; an audit trail that detects a changed entry; an invoice and its ledger entry staying in step; ledger integrity that can be re-verified. 3. The External Reporting Board (XRB), and the IAASB published by IFAC.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 2. Set up a training business
text: 1. So that nobody can hand out a login and lock the owner out of their own books. ByteBook requires the owner to have set a password before another sign-in can be switched on, and only the owner can open the security settings. 2. In ~/Library/Application Support/ByteBook/ on a Mac, or %APPDATA%\ByteBook\ on Windows, beside a backups folder holding the last thirty copies. 3. Understand is for reading what the business did; Set up is for changing how it is configured.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 3. The twelve businesses
text: 1. Bright Cuts has no GST. Marine Parade Rentals has exempt rent beside taxable supplies. 2. Any three of: every entry balances; every invoice's lines add up to its total; the GST in the return equals the GST in the ledger; the balance sheet balances; nothing is stored off the cent; a void cancels itself out; the fingerprint chain has no breaks; the assurance programme reports no exceptions (it may still carry notes for information). 3. More transactions fall inside one return, so a single misfiled or miscoded transaction distorts the whole period, and the reconciliation has more to prove.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 4. Invoices
text: 1. August, because that is when the performance obligation is satisfied. Money received in June is not revenue; it is an amount owed back in services. 2. Posting creates the entry and moves the reports. A draft is only a document. 3. It removes the ambiguity about whether a price includes GST, so no report has to guess which way a number was meant.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 5. Payments and debtors
text: 1. $700 still owing, aged from the invoice date. That is right: the customer still owes it, and the ageing is what tells you how long they have owed it. 2. It usually means a payment was recorded against the wrong invoice or was recorded twice, so the total owed is right while the detail is wrong. 3. The standard requires the allowance for trade receivables to be measured at lifetime expected credit losses. What is left to judgement is the estimate itself — the rates and the identification of debts known to be bad.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 6. Bills, expenses and documents
text: 1. February, because that is when the service was consumed. The date the money left the bank does not decide when the expense belongs. 2. A change in estimate is recognised prospectively, in this period and future ones. A material prior period error is corrected retrospectively. 3. Whether it was an expense at all, or an asset. Above about $1,000 the procedure lists it and marks the round number; whether the description is vague, or the cost looks personal, is for you to notice when you read the entry.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 7. The bank statement
text: 1. No. The balance may agree while part of the period is unrecorded, so the reconciliation is incomplete even though the arithmetic works. 2. It was produced by the bank rather than by the business, so it is independent of the records it is being used to check. 3. Which account the payment was for. The bank line is the cash that moved, GST included, and ByteBook takes any GST out of that amount; the account's own GST treatment decides whether there is any GST in it to take out.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 8. GST
text: 1. Invoice basis: the March return, because the invoice was issued in March. Payments basis: the May period, because that is when the money moved. 2. Box 5 is total sales and income including GST; box 8 is the GST itself. Confusing them overstates the tax owed, and they are different questions. 3. So that there is a record of what was filed, at the date it was worked out. If the ledger changes later, ByteBook can warn that the filed return no longer matches the books, and without a snapshot there is nothing to compare against.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 9. Reading the reports
text: 1. Because GST collected was never the business's income; it is held on behalf of Inland Revenue until the return is filed. 2. Because a figure that should be zero is the fastest way to see that something is wrong. Stating a difference rather than hiding it turns a silent failure into a visible one. 3. Nothing appears in Money in and out for the purchase, because no cash moved. In a full statement of cash flows the purchase would be disclosed separately as a non-cash investing and financing transaction.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 10. Closing a period
text: 1. The order in the chapter, with bank coding and reconciliation before the GST return, because the return is built from the transactions: an uncoded bank line is a transaction the return has not seen. Reproducing the reports should come after every adjustment, so that the check tests the final figures. 2. Adjusting. The customer's difficulty existed at the reporting date; the liquidation is evidence of a condition that was already there, so the amounts are adjusted. 3. Stock is written down by $2,500 to its net realisable value of $5,500, and the write-down is an expense in the period.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 11. Nothing is deleted
text: 1. The record of what was posted, and therefore the ability of anybody else to agree with the corrected figure. 2. Because a voided entry keeps the fingerprint it was sealed with. The correction is a new entry; nothing about the old one changes. 3. That an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit can understand the procedures performed, their results, the evidence obtained, and the significant matters and judgements.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 12. The audit trail and the chain
text: 1. Because altering one entry breaks every fingerprint after it, so a change cannot be made quietly in the middle of the record. 2. That the record has not been altered since it was written. It does not prove that the entries are correct, or that they were posted to the right accounts. 3. Because the correction is part of the history. Removing it would break the chain and destroy the record an accountant expects to see.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 13. The sixteen procedures
text: 1. Because they call for different actions. An exception needs somebody to look at it and decide something; information is something you should know. Collapsing the two would either hide real findings or manufacture work. 2. A09, cut-off, which reports entries dated inside a period that has already been packed and closed. 3. No. The procedure reports what it found and leaves the conclusion to the person. Four exceptions are four questions, not a verdict.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 14. Sealed packs and working papers
text: 1. The pack's fingerprint fails to verify, and it is detected the next time the pack is verified, because the fingerprint is recomputed from the ledger as it stands now. 2. Because a void moves the period's totals. The correction is legitimate and the period has still changed after it was sealed, and the pack is designed to detect exactly that. 3. ByteBook can test that the two sides of every entry are equal and that the figures on the reports can be reproduced from the rows. It cannot judge whether a debt will be collected or whether a provision is adequate.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 15. Roles and access
text: 1. So that no role can be created that locks the owner out, and so that every role that exists was created deliberately by someone with the highest level of access. 2. Objectivity, which requires judgement without bias, conflict of interest or undue influence. A read-only login removes the question rather than relying on trust. 3. Who can sign in, when the books were last backed up, and whether anything failed quietly. It belongs in the programme because an auditor relies on the system, so how the system is controlled and who can reach it are relevant to that reliance.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 16. Reading a standard reference
text: 1. That it is the New Zealand version of an international standard: the IAASB's ISA 230 with New Zealand additions, issued by the XRB. 2. Because it names one specific requirement that a reader can find in a minute and check. A reference to a topic cannot be re-performed. 3. That the publisher's document at that address is no longer the copy this handbook was checked against — most likely a new version. Read the current version before relying on the reference.

chapterTitle: Answers to the check-yourself questions
title: 20. How this handbook stays accurate
text: 1. Every reference must name a standard that is in the library; every quoted paragraph must be found in the publisher's own text; and every document must still match the SHA-256 recorded when it was downloaded. 2. Because it is more likely to be believed. An obviously old handbook invites checking; a confident wrong one is followed. 3. Because a working paper about an earlier period still has to cite the rule that applied then.

chapterTitle: Glossary
title: Glossary
text: Accrual basis. Recording income and expenses when they are earned or incurred, not when the money moves. A business using the accrual basis can be profitable and short of cash at the same time. Adjusting event. Something that happens after balance date that provides evidence of a condition existing at balance date. The amounts in the accounts are adjusted for it. Aged debtors. Money owed by customers, grouped by how long it has been owed. Assurance. The work an auditor or reviewer does to reach a conclusion about information somebody else prepared. Audit trail. The record of what was entered, when, by whom, and what was done about it. In ByteBook it is a chain of fingerprints. Audit key. A named, revocable, read-only key that lets an auditor's own tools read the audit data through the API. It cannot post, change or delete anything, and every use is written to the access log. Balance sheet. A statement of what a business owns and owes at a date. Also called the statement of financial position. Bill. A supplier's invoice that you will pay later. Until it is paid it sits in creditors. Chain (the). ByteBook's page showing the record at three scales: a ribbon of every day on a time axis
